title: Introduction to Calculus
summary: A gentle introduction to calculus: rates of change and limits, derivatives and the power rule, maxima and minima in real problems, the calculus of motion, integration and area, and real-world applications. Every result was checked with a computer algebra system.
audience: Senior secondary students, first-year students and adults preparing for science, engineering or economics

body.p: Calculus is the mathematics of change. It lets us find instantaneous rates (how fast something changes at a moment) and accumulated totals (how much builds up over time). It is used in physics, engineering, economics, biology and data science.

The average rate of change of f between two points is the gradient of the line joining them: (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a). For f(x) = x² from x = 1 to x = 3: (9 - 1) / 2 = 4. If f gave distance and x time, this would be the average speed.

To find the rate at a single instant, we let the interval shrink towards zero. A limit is the value a quantity approaches. For example, (x² - 4) / (x - 2) is undefined at x = 2, but as x approaches 2 the expression approaches 4, because it simplifies to x + 2 when x is not 2.
Applying this idea, the gradient of x² at any point is the limit of ((x + h)² - x²) / h as h approaches 0, which equals 2x. At x = 3 the gradient is 6.

body.tip: Think of a limit as "where the values are heading", not necessarily the value at the point itself.

body.p: The derivative f'(x) (or dy/dx) gives the instantaneous rate of change: the gradient of the tangent to the curve at each point.

list: Power rule: the derivative of xⁿ is nxⁿ⁻¹. The derivative of x² is 2x; of x³ is 3x².
Constant multiple: the derivative of 3x⁴ is 12x³; at x = 2 that is 12 x 8 = 96.
Sum rule: differentiate term by term. The derivative of 5x³ - 2x + 7 is 15x² - 2.
The derivative of a constant is 0, because a constant does not change.
More advanced rules (product, quotient and chain rules) handle products and compositions of functions.

body.p: If C(x) is the cost of producing x items, C'(x) is the marginal cost: roughly the cost of one more item. If s(t) is position, s'(t) is velocity.

body.tip: Lower the power by one and multiply by the old power; practise until it is automatic.

body.p: At the top of a hill or the bottom of a valley on a smooth curve, the gradient is zero. Setting the derivative to zero finds these stationary points, which solve many optimisation problems.

A farmer has 100 m of fencing for a rectangular pen. If one side is x, the other is 50 - x, so the area is A = x(50 - x) = 50x - x². A'(x) = 50 - 2x = 0 gives x = 25. The best pen is a 25 m by 25 m square with area 625 m².
If profit is P = -2x² + 40x (in thousands of rand, for x hundred units), P'(x) = -4x + 40 = 0 gives x = 10, and P(10) = -200 + 400 = 200, a maximum profit of R200 000.

list: Check whether a stationary point is a maximum or minimum, for example by the sign of the second derivative (negative means maximum).
Also check the ends of any allowed range of x.

body.tip: Write the quantity to optimise in terms of one variable before differentiating.

body.p: Derivatives connect position, velocity and acceleration.

list: Velocity is the derivative of position: v = ds/dt.
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity: a = dv/dt.
If s = t³ metres, then v = 3t² and a = 6t. At t = 2 s, the velocity is 12 m/s and the acceleration is 12 m/s².
When velocity is zero, the object is momentarily at rest, such as a ball at the top of its flight.

body.p: Going the other way, integrating velocity gives distance. A car with velocity v = 10 - 2t m/s slows to a stop at t = 5 s; the distance travelled is the area under the velocity graph from 0 to 5, which is 25 m.

body.tip: Remember the chain: position → (differentiate) → velocity → (differentiate) → acceleration; integrate to go back.

body.p: Integration reverses differentiation and measures accumulation, such as total distance from velocity or total area under a curve.

list: The integral of xⁿ is xⁿ⁺¹ / (n + 1) + C, for n not equal to -1.
∫(2x + 1) dx = x² + x + C. The constant C appears because constants vanish when differentiated.
Check by differentiating your answer: the derivative of x² + x is 2x + 1.

body.p: A definite integral gives the area under a curve between two limits: ∫₀³ x² dx = [x³/3] from 0 to 3 = 27/3 - 0 = 9. Similarly, ∫₁⁴ 2x dx = [x²] from 1 to 4 = 16 - 1 = 15.

The fundamental theorem of calculus links the two halves of calculus: the definite integral of a rate of change gives the total change. Integration is used to find volumes, work done, total revenue from a rate of sales, and probabilities.

body.tip: For definite integrals, no + C is needed; subtract the value at the lower limit from the value at the upper limit.

list: Physics and engineering: motion, forces, electrical circuits and the strength of structures.
Economics: marginal cost and revenue, maximising profit and minimising cost.
Biology and medicine: population growth, how drug concentrations rise and fall in the body, and the spread of disease.
Data science and AI: training machine-learning models uses derivatives (gradient descent) to reduce errors step by step.
Finance: continuously compounded interest and modelling changing prices.

body.p: Further calculus includes the product, quotient and chain rules, derivatives of exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions, integration techniques and differential equations, which describe how quantities change, such as cooling, growth and oscillations.
Calculus rests on algebra, so strong skills in expanding, factorising and rearranging make it much easier.

body.tip: Sketch graphs alongside calculations; seeing the curve, its gradient and its area builds real understanding.
